title: Two cultures
hookLine: raising children between Punjab and wherever you live
tomorrow: Maya's family looks nothing like Simran's. is there room for them?

lines: WHY DO I HAVE TO LEARN PUNJABI?
cards: Some kids have two lunchboxes in their head: the one they bring to school, and the one they'd never bring. Over breakfast, Fateh pushes his Gurmukhi workbook away. Nobody at school learns Punjabi, he says.
Why do I have to? Massi looks at Simran. Simran, who leaves for college in a year and has been asking herself the same thing lately, puts down her tea and takes the question seriously.

teach.b: Gurmukhi is the script the Guru Granth Sahib is written in, and tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping it and teaching it.
So the letters in Fateh's workbook are the door to reading the Gurus in their own words, at Bebe's kitchen table or anywhere on earth. That's Simran's first answer.

teach.h: YOU DON'T HAVE TO PICK A LUNCHBOX.
teach.b: Her second: you don't have to pick a lunchbox. Two cultures, Punjab and California, can both be home, the way the Granth itself holds the verses of Guru Nanak beside saints like Kabir and Farid, from other backgrounds.

teach.h: TWO WEEKS OF TWO WORLDS MEETING.
teach.b: And the last two weeks were full of two worlds meeting. Rounds walked as a map for two. One light in two bodies.
Patience at home after a fight. Tea poured for a daughter-in-law first. A living room turned small sangat.
Bebe reading while Harjit snored. None of that is only Punjab and none of it is only California.
It's a family carrying something old into a new place, a word at a time. Fateh pulls the workbook back.
Fine, he says. But you have to learn one too. Simran agrees.
Her letter for the day is the one that starts his name.

how: Some gurdwaras outside Punjab run Punjabi and Gurmukhi classes for children, and families mix the languages and customs of both places at home.

games.q: your kid says, 'i'm american, not punjabi. why do i have to pick?' what's Simran's answer from today?
o: you don't have to pick; both can be home, carried a word at a time.
you have to pick one, so pick the one your parents chose.
pick the one your friends have; that's where you really live.
games.why: Simran: you don't have to pick a lunchbox. two worlds, one family, the way the Granth holds voices from more than one background.

practice: Take a pen and write, by hand, one word from a language your family carries, or one word you'd want passed on to someone younger. Write it slowly, letter by letter, the way Fateh traces his workbook.
Then rest your hand on the page for the sit.
